Neurons are the basic unit of the nervous system...

Dendrites are short thread-like branches which act to accept nerve impulses from other neurons and carry them towards the cell body, which is the main part of the cell, containing the nucleus and other organelles
Axons are longer branches which carry nerve impulses away from the cell body
A myelin sheath surrounds many axons, insulating the neuron and speeding up the rate of impulse transmission.
Schwann Cells, a type of glial cell, are responsible for producing the myelin that surrounds each axon.

In myelinated axons, gaps between Schwann cells are referred to as the nodes of Ranvier. Electrical impulses “jump” from node to node, which is referred to as saltatory conduction. This speeds up transmission, avoiding having to travel down the entire length of the axon.
Once the electrical signal reaches the axon terminal, it is then passed on to the dendrites of an adjoining neuron.
Synapse: the space/junction between two adjoining neurons

A nerve impulse or action potential has both a chemical and electrical component (hence the term electrochemical impulse)
Four stages of a nerve impulse:
The difference in charge across the membrane of a resting neuron is called resting membrane potential.
The inside of a neuron has a slight negative charge at rest, whereas the outside has a slight positive charge.
This results in a resting potential of -70 mV in most neurons
Note: we often use specific numbers for voltages in our examples, but these can change from one neuron to another
Inside the resting cell, there exists a higher concentration of potassium (K+) than sodium (Na+); outside the cell, the opposite is true.
Potassium ions are able to passively diffuse out of the cell more easily than sodium ions can diffuse into the (K+ = “leaky” ion channels)
In an attempt to balance this difference, the sodium-potassium pump along the membrane surface will pump two K+ back into the cell in exchange for three Na+

As a result, as excess of positive charge accumulates outside of the cell membrane, causing the inside of the cell to become negatively charged relative to the outside. A constant membrane potential of -70 mV is maintained.
Action potential occurs when a neuron is stimulated by an electrical impulse.
If a strong enough impulse is received and the threshold potential is reached (approx. -55 mV), sodium gates will open, thus allowing Na+ to diffuse freely across the membrane.
Na+ rushes into the cell (down their concentration gradient → facilitated diffusion), leading to a slight positive charge on the inside relative to the outside.
This reverses the membrane potential from -70 mV to +40 mV; the membrane is now said to be depolarized.
Once Na+ reaches equilibrium, the membrane once again becomes impermeable to them, and the gates close.
An action potential is considered to be an “all-or-none” event because any stimulus that fails to achieve the threshold membrane potential of at least -55 mV will have no effect
Note that increasing the stimulus strength does not increase the impulse strength; a neuron will either fire or not fire
The intensity of a stimulus is instead experienced as an increased frequency of nerve impulses (i.e. a more intense stimulus will simply cause more neurons to depolarize)
Once the action potential has peaked, Na+ gates close, and K+ gates open.
This restores the positive charge on the outside of the membrane; however, Na+ and K+ concentrations are briefly reversed compared to at the resting state (Na+ is higher inside the membrane)
The K+ channels are slow to close, which results in the hyperpolarization of the neuron. This means that the inside becomes slightly more negative than the resting potential.
Na+/K+ exchange pump helps reset the correct distribution of ions

Even though during repolarization the inside becomes more negative again compared to the outside, we do not have the correct distribution of Na+ and K+ across the membrane. The sodium-potassium exchange pump helps reset the original distribution by pumping 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ it pumps in.
Nerve transmission occurs in a wave-like pattern down the length of the axon.
Until the resting potential of the neuron has been properly restored, a second action potential cannot be conducted along the axon; this is referred to as the refractory period.
During this time, the membrane cannot be made permeable to Na+, so a second wave of depolarization cannot occur.

Signal Transduction across a Synapse (Chemical Event)
Once the impulse has traveled down the length of the axon, it reaches the axon terminal.
The axon terminal is in close contact with the dendrites of another neuron.
For the signal to move to the next neuron, it must cross the space between the axon terminal and the dendrites of the subsequent cell; this space is referred to as the synapse.
An action potential reaches the axon terminal
Calcium channel “gates” within the axon terminal open, causing calcium ions to flow into the cell
Calcium ions trigger the movement and fusing of the vesicles with the presynaptic membrane (exocytosis). In turn, neurotransmitters are released into the synapse.
Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft to the post-synaptic membrane
Neurotransmitters are required to help transmit the electrical impulse from one neuron to another. These are stored in vesicles in the axon bulb.
Once neurotransmitters have reached the post-synaptic membrane, they bind with receptors embedded in the membrane
If the neurotransmitter is excitatory, binding induces an action potential in the postsynaptic neuron
Neurotransmitters are then released by the receptors and either return to the presynaptic neuron or are broken down by enzymes such as cholinesterase on the post-synaptic membrane

cause the sodium channels of the post-synaptic membrane to open and sodium to flow in, resulting in slight depolarization of the membrane and lowering the threshold potential of the post-synaptic neuron
e.g. acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter found in muscle cells; it excites the muscle membrane, causing depolarization and contraction of the muscle fibre
Cholinesterase (an enzyme) is required to break down acetylcholine after the action potential has occurred

Often when more than one neuron fires at the same time, a sufficient amount of neurotransmitter is released to cause depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane. The production of an action potential as a result is referred to as summation

Extra: The Stress Response and Anxiety

The stress response, which triggers when our bodies perceive a threat, served an important evolutionary purpose in helping our ancestors survive dangerous situations. However, in modern times, stressors often aren't physical threats but rather psychological ones like exams, social pressures, or work deadlines. While the stress response can still help us cope with these challenges, if it's triggered too frequently or intensely, it can lead to chronic stress and anxiety. This is because our bodies aren't designed to handle prolonged periods of stress, and the constant activation of the stress response can have negative effects on both our physical and mental health, contributing to conditions like anxiety disorders.

Damage to the CNS can affect everything from temperament and motor control to the maintenance of homeostasis depending on which region is harmed.
The CNS consists of two types of nervous tissue: grey matter (unmyelinated neurons) & white matter (myelinated neurons)
Composed of the brain and spinal cord, the central nervous system is the site of neural integration and processing.
The spinal cord provides a vital link for communication between the brain and peripheral nervous system…
Each segment of the spinal cord is responsible for specific functions.
(Note: you don’t need to memorize the specific regions or what they affect)
The delicate tissues of the spinal cord are protected by cerebrospinal fluid and a series of vertebrae.
Injury to areas of the spinal column closer to the brain results in the loss of more functions compared to injury of areas closer to the abdomen.

Paraplegia: If the injury occurs below the first thoracic vertebrae in the upper back region, the paralysis is likely to be confined to the legs. A paraplegic patient will retain full use of their arms and hands.

Quadriplegia: If the injury occurs above the first thoracic vertebrae in the cervical vertebrae or neck region of the body, the paralysis generally results in loss of movement in all limbs. Abdominal and chest muscles may also be affected, resulting in weakened breathing and the inability to properly cough to clear the chest.
A spinal cord injury usually results in the area of the body below the injury site being partially or completely unable to communicate with the brain.
Paraplegic patients are not necessarily confined to a wheelchair; modern prosthetics and stem cell treatment can provide an increased level of mobility
The brain is the center for intelligence, consciousness, and emotion. It also regulates bodily functions without conscious thought (e.g. breathing).
Enclosed within the skull, the brain is surrounded by a tough three-layer membrane known as the meninges.
Cerebrospinal fluid circulates between the meninges and the spinal cord, acting as a shock absorber and a transport medium, carrying nutrients & waste to and from brain cells.

The forebrain or cerebrum is the largest part of the brain. It is divided into left and right hemispheres, and can be further categorized into four main lobes, each of which is responsible for a series of specific functions.
The surface of the cerebrum is referred to as the cerebral cortex. Composed of grey matter, the cortex has many folds which act to increase surface area.

The left-hemisphere tends to be more analytical & concrete, while the right-hemisphere tends to be more creative & abstract
However, there is a great degree of overlap and interaction between the
Communication between the two hemispheres occurs via the corpus callosum and is essential for integrating these functions
Damage to the brain can lead to impairments in language, or aphasia.
Depending on which area is damaged, patients may experience difficulties with language production (Broca’s Aphasia) or language comprehension (Wernicke’s Aphasia).
In Broca’s Aphasia, patients are unable to produce fluent speech despite understanding what others are saying.
In Wernicke’s Aphasia, patients are able to produce fluent speech, but do not actually understand what they are saying/what is being said to them, so their words often do not make sense.
Patients with Broca’s Aphasia can learn to speak through song, as the area of the brain responsible for singing is different than the area responsible for speech.
